cards.explanation: The answer is False. The commander released Paul, then brought him down and had him stand before the council. He wanted to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews (Acts 22:30). Being let out of a tight spot is a feeling I know well, friends.

The answer is that his conscience has been good to this day. Paul says, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” (Acts 23:1) Look at where he puts it, friends: before God, not just before the council. That's a bold way to start when he's looking directly at the Sanhedrin.

The answer is high priest. The text calls Ananias the high priest. He's the one who ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth (Acts 23:2). That's a heavy moment, friends, and I think Paul felt it.

The answer is by ordering that Paul be struck. Paul says, “You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck.” (Acts 23:3) His point is that the one judging by the law is the one who commanded the strike. A judge who breaks the rule while holding the rulebook is a hard thing to defend, friends.

The answer is True. Paul replies, “I was not aware that he was the high priest…” Then he quotes what is written: “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” (Acts 23:5) He answers the charge by pointing to Scripture, friends.

The answer is to not speak evil about the ruler of your people. Paul quotes what is written: “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” (Exodus 22:28; Acts 23:5) He says it right after the people nearby object to how he talked to the high priest. He brings the Word to the room, friends, and that's a good way to answer.

The answer is that a dispute splits the Pharisees and Sadducees. As soon as Paul said it, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided (Acts 23:7). One line from Paul and the room splits in two. I've seen a crowd argue over the last cookie, but not like this, bakers.

The answer is that the Sadducees say there is no resurrection. The Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all (Acts 23:8). Paul says he's on trial because of his hope in the resurrection of the dead. That's the exact spot where the two groups disagree, friends.

The answer is True. The Pharisees acknowledge them all: the resurrection, angels and spirits. The Sadducees say there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits (Acts 23:8). Same room, two different answers, friends.

The answer is False. The scribes from the party of the Pharisees get up and contend sharply, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” (Acts 23:9) They aren't asking for punishment at all. For a moment, friends, a few of them are on Paul's side.

The answer is that a spirit or an angel spoke to him. The scribes ask, “What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” (Acts 23:9) They say it right after, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” It's a question, friends, and the text leaves it as one.

The answer is barracks. The commander orders the soldiers to go down, remove Paul by force and bring him into the barracks. The dispute grew so violent that he was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces (Acts 23:10). That's a rough way to end the meeting, bakers, and I think it was a scary moment.

The answer is False. The Lord stands near Paul and says, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.” (Acts 23:11) Jerusalem isn't the end of it, bakers. Rome is still ahead.
